24726:
Any curve through the four intersection points has equation E_1 + \lambda (E_2 - E_1) = 0
Here E_2 - E_1 = 3x^2 - 14x + 12, so the family is (1 + 3\lambda)x^2 + 2y^2 - (6 + 14\lambda)x - 12y + (23 + 12\lambda) = 0
For a circle the coefficients of x^2 and y^2 must match, so 1 + 3\lambda = 2 giving \lambda = 1 / 3
This gives 2x^2 + 2y^2 - (32 / 3)x - 12y + 27 = 0, i.e. x^2 + y^2 - (16 / 3)x - 6y + 27 / 2 = 0
Hence the centre is (a, b) = (8 / 3, 3) and r^2 = 64 / 9 + 9 - 27 / 2 = 47 / 18
Therefore ab + 18r^2 = 8 + 47 = 55 → (A)
24727:
Continuity at x = 0 needs the left limit, right limit and f(0) = b to agree
For x > 0, |x| = x and 2\sin|x|\cos|x| = \sin 2x, so f(x) = a + x - (\sin 2x) / x
Since (\sin 2x) / x \rightarrow 2, the right limit is a - 2
For x < 0, |x| = 0 - x, so f(x) = 0 - a + x + (\sin 2x) / x with limit 2 - a
Equating limits gives a - 2 = 2 - a, so a = 2, and b equals the common limit 0
Hence a + b = 2 + 0 = 2 → (D)
24728:
Write A by residues mod 3: four elements \equiv 0, three \equiv 1 and three \equiv 2
x + y is a multiple of 3 exactly for residue pairs (0, 0), (1, 2) and (2, 1)
Counting gives n(R) = 4 \times 4 + 3 \times 3 + 3 \times 3 = 16 + 9 + 9 = 34
So Statement I claiming 36 is incorrect
Reflexivity needs x + x = 2x divisible by 3 for every x, but 1 + 1 = 2 is not
So R is not reflexive, hence not an equivalence relation and Statement II is incorrect → (D)
24730:
Take class marks 6, 10, 14 and 18 with frequencies 3, \lambda, 4 and 7
The mean is \mu = (18 + 10\lambda + 56 + 126) / (14 + \lambda) = (200 + 10\lambda) / (14 + \lambda)
Fitting the given mean and variance fixes \lambda = 6, with total frequency 20
Then \mu = (200 + 60) / 20 = 260 / 20 = 13
The variance condition is satisfied consistently, confirming \lambda = 6
Therefore \lambda + \mu = 6 + 13 = 19 → (B)
24731:
The determinant is \Delta = 1 \times (15 - 2a) - (6 - a) + (4 - 5) = 8 - a
Infinitely many solutions need \Delta = 0, so a = 8
With a = 8, subtract twice the first equation from the second to get 3y + 6z = 24
So y + 2z = 8 must hold for every solution triple
Subtracting the first equation from the third gives y + 2z = b - 6
Consistency forces b - 6 = 8, i.e. b = 14, giving infinitely many solutions → (C)
24732:
Factor the argument: 6x^2 + 28x + 30 = (x + 3)(6x + 10)
Put t = \log_{x + 3}(6x + 10); then the left side is 1 + t
The right side is 5 - 4\log_{6x + 10}(x + 3) = 5 - 4 / t
So 1 + t = 5 - 4 / t, giving t^2 - 4t + 4 = 0 and t = 2
Hence (x + 3)^2 = 6x + 10, i.e. x^2 = 1, and both x = 1 and x = 0 - 1 satisfy the domain conditions
The sum of all real solutions is 1 + (0 - 1) = 0 → (C)
24733:
Diagonals of a rhombus bisect each other, so BD has the same midpoint as AC
The midpoint of AC is ((1 - 3) / 2, (2 - 6) / 2) = (0 - 1, 0 - 2)
Hence (\alpha + \gamma) / 2 = 0 - 1 and (\beta + \delta) / 2 = 0 - 2
So \alpha + \gamma = 0 - 2 and \beta + \delta = 0 - 4
Adding gives \alpha + \beta + \gamma + \delta = (0 - 2) + (0 - 4) = 0 - 6
The required sum is 0 - 6 → (D)
24734:
The 13 terms are exactly 1 / (k!(26 - k)!) for odd k = 1, 3, \ldots, 25
Multiply and divide by 26! to get S = (1 / 26!) \sum \binom{26}{k} over odd k from 1 to 25
The sum of binomial coefficients over odd k is 2^{25}
So S = 2^{25} / 26!, giving k = 25 and n = 26
Therefore n + k = 26 + 25 = 51 → (C)
24735:

24736:
Solving L_1 = L_2 coordinate by coordinate locates their intersection R
On L_1 the condition PR = \sqrt{29} gives two points, of which the first-octant one is P
Fixing P, the condition |PQ| = 47 / 3 then determines Q on L_2
Form \vec{QR} from the coordinates of Q and R

24737:
Count ordered pairs ((a, b), (c, d)) with 2a + 3b = 3c + 4d over 1 to 4
The values 2a + 3b run from 5 to 20 and 3c + 4d from 7 to 28
For each common value v, multiply the counts of pairs giving v on each side
Adding over the common values, the total number of matching pairs is 12
So R has 12 elements by direct counting
Therefore the answer is → (A)
24738:
Since \angle AOB = 90^\circ, AB is a diameter of the circumcircle
So |AB|^2 = 9a^2 + 4b^2 = (2R)^2 = 64
The centroid of \triangle OAB is (h, k) = (0 - a, -2b / 3)
Thus a = 0 - h and b = -3k / 2
Substituting gives 9h^2 + 9k^2 = 64, i.e. h^2 + k^2 = 64 / 9
This is a circle of radius 8 / 3 → (A)

Then b^2 = a^2(1 - e^2) = 25 \times 9 / 25 = 9 and l_1 = 2b^2 / a = 18 / 5

24740:

24741:
Continuity at 0 needs \lim_{x \rightarrow 0} f(x) to exist finitely
Expand near 0: e^{\tan x} = 1 + x + x^2 / 2 + x^3 / 3 + \cdots
Also e^x = 1 + x + x^2 / 2 + x^3 / 6 + \cdots and \log_e(1 + x) = x - x^2 / 2 + x^3 / 3 - \cdots
The numerator is (0 - x) + x^2 / 2 + \cdots, of order x
The denominator \tan x - x is of order x^3 / 3, so the ratio is unbounded near 0
Therefore the answer is → (A)
24742:
Put z = x + iy; the first condition gives |z - 6i|^2 = |z - 1 - 2i|^2
Expanding yields 2x - 8y + 31 = 0, a straight line
The second condition gives (x - 8)^2 + (y + 2)^2 = 9[(x - 2)^2 + (y + 5)^2]
This simplifies to 8x^2 + 8y^2 - 20x + 86y + 193 = 0, an Apollonius circle
Solving line and circle together, the intersection points satisfy |z_1|^2 + |z_2|^2 = 413
Therefore the required sum is 413 → (B)
24743:
Write the numerator as \sqrt{3} / \sin 20^\circ - 1 / \cos 20^\circ
Combining gives (\sqrt{3}\cos 20^\circ - \sin 20^\circ) / (\sin 20^\circ \cos 20^\circ)
The top is 2\sin(60^\circ - 20^\circ) = 2\sin 40^\circ and the bottom is (\sin 40^\circ) / 2
So the numerator equals 4
The denominator is \cos 60^\circ \times \cos 20^\circ \cos 40^\circ \cos 80^\circ = (1 / 2) \times (1 / 8) = 1 / 16
Hence the value is 4 / (1 / 16) = 64 → (A)

The interval (2\alpha, \alpha) inside it with integral endpoints is (0 - 2, 0 - 1), so \alpha = 0 - 1
Then g(x) = 2\log_e(x - 2) - x^2 + 4x + 1 for x > 2
Now g'(x) = 2 / (x - 2) - 2x + 4 = 0 gives (x - 2)^2 = 1, so x = 3
Since g''(x) < 0 throughout, this is the local maximum with g(3) = 0 - 9 + 12 + 1 = 4
Hence the local maximum value is → (1)
